title: Iberia Airlines 610

agencies.name: Civil Aviation Accident and Incident Investigation Commission

summary: Iberia Flight 610, a Boeing 727 on a short domestic hop from Madrid to Bilbao, crashed into a ravine on Mount Oiz on 19 February 1985 after its left wing struck a television antenna during the approach in fog, killing all 141 passengers and 7 crew. Spanish investigators found the autopilot's altitude-select system had failed to engage, letting the aircraft descend past its target altitude, and that the crew misread the altitude alerts and kept descending during a turn that took them into the fog-shrouded mountain.
probable_cause: Spanish investigators attributed the crash to pilot error: the autopilot's altitude select system failed to engage for undetermined reasons, and the crew misinterpreted the altitude alarms, continuing a descent below safe altitude during a turn that flew the aircraft into Mount Oiz in fog.

factors.evidence: The autopilot's altitude select system failed to engage due to undetermined reasons, enabling the aircraft to descend past its target altitude.
The altitude alert went off and the crew continued the descent as the second tonal alarm, which would have confirmed level-off, had not sounded.
The weather conditions at the time were cloudy with fog, with 4 km of visibility, as the aircraft flew 177 ft above Mount Oiz.
The crew began to initiate the loop back towards the airport by making a tight turn to the left, during which they would bypass Mount Oiz.
The aircraft's left wing collided with an antenna of the Euskal Telebistarues television tower at 3,356 ft, shearing the wing off and causing the aircraft to crash into a ravine.

events.text: During the approach the autopilot's altitude select system failed to engage for undetermined reasons, letting the aircraft descend past its target altitude.
The altitude alert sounded but the crew continued the descent because the second tonal alarm, which would have confirmed reaching the intended altitude, had not sounded.
The crew began a tight turn to the left to loop back toward the airport, a maneuver intended to bypass Mount Oiz, while flying in fog with 4 km of visibility.
Flying 177 ft above Mount Oiz in landing configuration at 239 mph, the aircraft's left wing collided with an antenna of the Euskal Telebistarues television tower at 3,356 ft.
Losing all lift from the left side, the aircraft rolled left, hit dozens of pine trees, and dived into a ravine in inverted condition, killing all 141 passengers and 7 crew.

title: Delta Air Lines 191
summary: Delta Air Lines Flight 191, an L-1011 TriStar, encountered a microburst while on approach to Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport on 2 August 1985. The aircraft impacted terrain over 1 mile short of the runway. The NTSB determined the crash resulted from the crew's decision to fly through a thunderstorm, the lack of procedures or training to avoid or escape microbursts, and the lack of hazard information on wind shear. The descent rate exceeded 3000 feet per minute with angle of attack over 30 degrees.
probable_cause: The National Transportation Safety Board determined that the crash resulted from the flight crew's decision to fly through a thunderstorm, the lack of procedures or training to avoid or escape microbursts and the lack of hazard information on wind shear.

title: Arrow Air 1285R
summary: Arrow Air Flight 1285R stalled and crashed shortly after takeoff from Gander, Newfoundland on December 12, 1985. The aircraft had accumulated ice contamination on the wings' leading edges during its earlier approach and refueling stop at Gander. The aircraft was not de-iced prior to takeoff, and the ice buildup degraded lift, resulting in a stall at low altitude from which recovery was not possible.
probable_cause: The most probable cause of the stall was ice contamination on the leading edge and upper surface of the wing following freezing precipitation exposure without de-icing before takeoff, combined with high drag and reduced lift conditions and possibly underestimated onboard weight.

factors.evidence: The aircraft stalled at low altitude from which recovery was not possible.
Ice contamination on the leading edge and upper surface of the wing resulted from precipitation conditions favorable for ice formation and freezing and frozen precipitation.
Prior to takeoff the aircraft had not been de-iced despite exposure to freezing and frozen precipitation.
Underestimated onboard weight may have compounded the effects of the contamination.
A non-functioning cockpit area microphone went undetected for an indeterminate number of flights, and no steps on standard checklists tested its functionality.
The defect in the cockpit area microphone went undetected due to no testing procedure on standard checklists.

events.text: During approach to Gander, precipitation conditions were favorable for formation of ice on wings.
After landing, aircraft remained exposed to freezing and frozen precipitation without de-icing.
Aircraft began takeoff roll on runway 22, rotated at 167 knots after 51 seconds, showing difficulty gaining altitude.
Airspeed reached 172 knots then decreased; aircraft descended after crossing Trans-Canada Highway 900 feet from runway departure end.
Aircraft struck terrain just short of Gander Lake approximately 3500 feet beyond runway departure end, broke up and exploded.
